```{r cfcount}
## Study 1 agreement count: every cell-variant of the closed-form
## check (01-e9-closed-form.R), all designs and structures.
cfz <- read.csv(file.path('..', '..', 'data', 'quick-sim',
                          'carryover-closed-form', 'e9-closed-form-vs-mc.csv'))
cf_n <- nrow(cfz)
cf_beyond <- sum(abs(cfz$power_z) > 2)
cf_expect <- round(cf_n * 2 * pnorm(-2))
```

**Number of replicates.** Replicate counts were set by the precision
each comparison needs. In study 3, 1,000 null replicates give a
two-MCSE band of 0.036 to 0.064 for a single cell. Pooling 11
non-prognostic null cells gives the band of 0.046 to 0.054 used in
Stage 6. In study 1, a cell is flagged when the simulated and
closed-form values differ by more than 2 MCSE. Chance alone produces
this in about 4.6% of cells, or about `r cf_expect` of the `r cf_n`
cell-variants (three designs, three correlation structures, two
statistics); `r cf_beyond` were flagged. The cell-variants are not
independent, since each uses its own draws but the same designs.

**Random numbers.** Every cell, or chunk of a cell, sets its own seed
from a fixed rule: a function of the cell's parameters in study 1, a
shared seed per half-life (study 2a) or per design, sample size and
half-life (study 2b), and $20261007 + 1000 \times \text{cell} +
\text{chunk}$ in study 3. Results therefore do not depend on the
number of cores or the order in which chunks run. Both versions of the
starting code in study 2 use the same seeds. All analyses in study 3
are fitted to the same trials. The comparisons are therefore paired.
R's default Mersenne-Twister generator was used throughout.

**Failed fits.** In study 3, a fit that returned
an error was recorded as missing. In the reported run, failures
numbered 0 to 10 per analysis over 28,000 trials, and at most 0.3% in
any cell. In the first and second runs they numbered 0 to 12 and 0 to
7, and at most 0.6% and 0.4% in any cell.
In study 2
the starting pipeline returned an estimate for every replicate. No
correlation matrix was repaired in either version, because
$c_{bm} = 0.25$ lies below the compound-symmetry feasibility bound of
0.256. Study 1 does not fit models for the paired-difference
statistic, so it has no failures.

**Which form of the DGP each study used.** Study 1 and the closed-form
calculations build the cross-component correlation as
$c_1\rho^{\lvert w_t - w_s\rvert}$ (the separable form) where the
separable structure is named, and as the starting constants where
compound symmetry is named. Study 2 is the starting code and so the
starting structure. Study 3 was run three times, with the separable
form in every cell except the compound-symmetry curve and an analysis
half-life of 0.5 week. The first run used fixed path allocation (18,
18, 17, 17) and the compounding carryover rule on the mean. The second
run used carryover decaying from the last on-drug mean, the rule of
the recommended DGP, and also assigned each participant to a path at
random in every trial. Randomized allocation is a driver option, not
part of the recommended DGP as defined (Table \@ref(tab:spec)). The third
run is the recommended DGP as defined: the anchored carryover rule with
fixed allocation. It differs from the first run only in the carryover
rule and from the second only in the allocation, so the two effects
can be separated. The tables in Stage 6 are from the third run. The
first run is in Appendix C, Table \@ref(tab:prognosticfirst).

**Software.** R 4.6.1, with lme4 2.0.1 and lmerTest 3.2.1 for the
starting pipeline, nlme 3.1-169, mmrm 0.3.17, clubSandwich 0.7.0 and
MASS 7.3-65. In study 3 the binary-indicator analysis is fitted with `mmrm`
and a compound-symmetry covariance with Satterthwaite inference, not
with `lmer`. The two coincide when the within-person correlation is
non-negative.

**Exploratory status.** The stress test is exploratory. Its cells and
analyses were written down as a working protocol (Additional file 2). No analysis plan was fixed in advance, and the protocol
was revised as results came in. Two cells with a prognostic
association between the biomarker and baseline severity, and three
analyses, were added after the first results. Failed fits were first
counted as non-rejections and are now excluded from the denominator,
a change of at most 0.0025 in any rate. The study also compared the
analyses' power and selected one by a decision rule. That selection
was revised after results, is post hoc, and is reported in
Additional file 3, not here. Such post hoc changes
can favor one method in comparative simulation studies
[@pawel2024pitfalls], which is a further reason not to rank the
analyses here. This paper uses the
stress test only for what it shows about the DGP: which analyses are
valid under a prognostic biomarker, and what the optional features do
to size and power.

# Results

The Results are organized as stages. Each stage takes one element of
the DGP. It states the candidate choices and the evidence. It ends
with the choice made and the criterion it rests on. Table \@ref(tab:spec), at
the end, collects the choices.

## Stage 1. Feasibility of the joint distribution

The first question is whether the joint distribution exists for the
effect sizes a study simulates. Under compound symmetry the
correlation matrix is positive definite only for $c_{bm}$ below a
bound. Without carryover the bound is 0.256 in the Hybrid design. It
is 0.256 in the crossover and 0.262 in the
open-label-plus-blinded-discontinuation design. These values follow
from the feasibility bound with $M$ the starting response block.

But why is the bound so low? It is the condition that the biomarker's
squared multiple correlation on the whole response trajectory stays
below one. Under compound symmetry every visit's drug response shares
the same person-level factor. The biomarker therefore cannot be
correlated with the on-drug visits alone. Through that factor it is
correlated with the off-drug visits as well. The bound is low for two
reasons. The correlation profile switches between visits that the
structure ties together. The drug-response component also keeps its
full variance at off-drug visits. Stages 4 and 5 show how far a
serial correlation that decays with lag raises the bound. Even then,
an effect size of 0.6 is infeasible in 75% of the extended grid and
in every Hybrid cell (Appendix B.2, Table \@ref(tab:nonpd)).

When a matrix is infeasible, a DGP can either repair it or refuse it.
The starting code repairs it without a warning (Appendix B.2). A
repaired matrix simulates a different DGP from the one stated, and it
does not report which correlation changed. The recommended DGP
therefore stops and reports the cell as infeasible. The package
function `buildSigma()` does so by default (Appendix B.5). The choice
rests on the existence criterion. What the bound means in outcome
units, and what to do above it, are taken up in the planning section
and the Discussion.

## Stage 2. The biomarker-response correlation under carryover

This stage takes the correlation at off-drug visits. Power to
detect the interaction falls sharply under the constant rule once
carryover is introduced [@hendrickson2020]. In our 500-replicate rerun of
the starting code in the Hybrid design at $N = 70$ and
$c_{bm} = 0.25$ (Table \@ref(tab:patch)), power fell from 0.668 without
carryover to 0.126 at a half-life of 0.1 week. A 4,000-replicate rerun
of that cell gives `r sprintf('%.3f', m6a_p)` (below). No correlation
matrix
was repaired in that run, because 0.25 lies below the
compound-symmetry feasibility bound of 0.256. At that half-life only
0.1% of the drug effect remains a week after stopping.

Under the constant rule every off-drug visit in the Hybrid design
follows an exposure. With any positive half-life its drug-response
mean is positive, so $g_t = 1$. Hence $\bar g_{\text{off}} = 1$ and,
by Proposition 2,

$$
\beta_{bm:D}^{\text{E9}} = 0, \qquad
\beta_{bm:D}^{\text{E9b}} = -c_{bm}\frac{\sigma_{BR}}{\sigma_{bm}}\,
  \frac{1}{n_{\text{off}} + 1}
\qquad \text{for every } t_{1/2} > 0 .
$$

Power is a step function of the half-life (Table
\@ref(tab:closedform), Figure \@ref(fig:powerfig)). It takes its
no-carryover value at $t_{1/2} = 0$. It takes a constant value at
every positive half-life of practical interest, whether 0.1 week or
10. The exception below about 0.007 week is an artifact of
double-precision arithmetic in the starting code, not a property of
the DGP (Appendix B.1). For E9b the constant is 0.081. This value
comes from the baseline row, which alone keeps $g_t = 0$.

```{r m6data}
m6 <- read.csv(file.path('..', '..', 'data', 'quick-sim',
                         'hendrickson-problems', 'graded-patch',
                         'published-th0.1-reps4000.csv'))
m6_R <- sum(m6$reps)
m6_p <- sum(m6$rej) / m6_R
m6_se <- sqrt(m6_p * (1 - m6_p) / m6_R)
stopifnot(m6_R == 4000, all(m6$t_half == 0.1), sum(m6$repairs) == 0)
```

The binary-indicator analysis behaves the same way. In our reconstruction of
the starting DGP, the mean estimate falls from $-0.126$ to between
$-0.026$ and $-0.032$ at every positive half-life. Power falls from
0.63 to between 0.08 and 0.11 (500 replicates per cell). The
separately seeded run of the starting code reported above gives 0.126
at 0.1 week, against 0.080 for the reconstruction. The difference is
2.4 combined Monte Carlo SE (two-sided $p = 0.016$). The two
implementations share the parameters, the path allocation and the
analysis model. They differ in the random-number stream and in the
carryover rule on the mean. At 0.1 week the carryover rule leaves an
off-drug drug-response mean below 0.011 points under either rule, so
it cannot account for a difference of this size. We therefore reran
the starting code at 0.1 week with 4,000 new replicates (16 seeds not
used before). Power was
`r sprintf('%.3f', m6_p)` (MCSE `r sprintf('%.4f', m6_se)`), within
`r sprintf('%.1f', abs(m6_p - 0.080) / sqrt(m6_se^2 + 0.080 * 0.920 / 500))`
combined Monte Carlo SE of the reconstruction. Rerunning the stored
cell with its stored seed reproduces 0.126 exactly. The rerun is
therefore consistent with the reconstruction, and the value of 0.126
is consistent with a high draw of a 500-replicate run. We found no
difference between the two implementations that would explain it.

With a constant correlation, the biomarker moderates the on-drug and
post-baseline off-drug responses equally. No interaction remains among
the post-baseline visits. Only the baseline visit, where the
correlation is zero, still contrasts with the on-drug visits, which is
why E9b and the binary-indicator analysis keep a little power. The loss
of power under small carryover is therefore a property of the
correlation rule, not of carryover or of the designs.

```{r closedform}
cfv <- read.csv(file.path('..', '..', 'data', 'quick-sim',
                          'carryover-closed-form', 'e9-closed-form-vs-mc.csv'))
cfv <- cfv[cfv$design == 'Hybrid' & cfv$construct == 'CS' & cfv$c.bm == 0.25, ]
cf_th <- c(0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2)
cfv_shown <- cfv[cfv$rule %in% c('step', 'graded') & cfv$t_half %in% cf_th, ]
stopifnot(nrow(cfv_shown) == 24)
cf_row <- function(rule, v) {
  sapply(cf_th, function(h) {
    x <- cfv$power[cfv$rule == rule & cfv$variant == v & cfv$t_half == h]
    stopifnot(length(x) == 1)
    x
  })
}
tab <- data.frame(
  Rule = c('Constant', '', 'Decaying', ''),
  Statistic = rep(c('E9', 'E9b'), 2),
  rbind(cf_row('step', 'E9'), cf_row('step', 'E9b'),
        cf_row('graded', 'E9'), cf_row('graded', 'E9b')))
knitr::kable(tab, booktabs = TRUE, digits = 3,
  col.names = c('Correlation rule', 'Statistic', '0', '0.1', '0.2', '0.5', '1', '2'),
  caption = paste0('Closed-form power by carryover half-life (weeks). Hybrid design, $N = 70$, $c_{bm} = 0.25$, compound symmetry. Constant: the constant rule (constant correlation after first exposure). Decaying: the decaying rule (correlation decaying at the carryover half-life). E9: paired-difference statistic on post-baseline visits; E9b: the same with baseline counted as an off-drug visit, as in the binary-indicator analysis. Against Monte Carlo estimates (5,000 replicates per cell), ', sum(abs(cfv_shown$power_z) > 2), ' of the ', nrow(cfv_shown), ' cell-variants in this table differ by more than 2 Monte Carlo SE, and ', cf_beyond, ' of all ', cf_n, ' cell-variants of study 1 (about ', cf_expect, ' expected by chance).'))
```

```{r powerfig, fig.cap = 'Closed-form power (lines) against carryover half-life, with Monte Carlo estimates (points; 5,000 replicates per cell), under the constant rule (constant correlation after first exposure) and the decaying rule (correlation decaying at the carryover half-life). Hybrid design, $N = 70$, $c_{bm} = 0.25$, compound symmetry; left panel E9b, right panel E9.', out.width = '85%', fig.align = 'center'}
knitr::include_graphics('../../../docs/figures/37-fig1-power-closed-form-cov.png')
```

The candidate is a correlation that decays after discontinuation at
the carryover half-life: $g_t = 1$ on drug, $2^{-t_{sd,t}/t_{1/2}}$
off drug after exposure, and 0 before any exposure. This is the
pharmacological reading of a predictive biomarker. The biomarker
predicts the size of the drug effect, so it cannot predict a drug
effect that is no longer present. Under the decaying rule the mean of
$g_t$ over the off-drug visits is

$$
\bar g_{\text{off}}(t_{1/2}) = \frac{1}{n_{\text{off}}}
  \sum_{t\,\text{off}} 2^{-t_{sd,t}/t_{1/2}},
$$

which is strictly increasing in $t_{1/2}$, because every off-drug visit
has $t_{sd} \ge 1$ week. Two consequences follow.

- **Power is strictly decreasing in the half-life** for the
  path-stratified paired-difference statistic. This holds on every
  path with at least one off-drug visit after an exposure (Proposition
  3, Appendix A.3). The placebo-first crossover path, whose off-drug
  visits all precede exposure, has constant power. For the pooled
  statistic power is non-increasing at every step of a 120-point grid
  from 0.03 to 4 weeks. For the binary-indicator mixed model only the
  simulated half-lives are available, and its values there are
  consistent with a monotone decline within Monte Carlo error (Table
  \@ref(tab:patch)).
- **The loss vanishes faster than any power of the half-life as
  $t_{1/2} \to 0$.** At 0.1 week, $\bar g_{\text{off}} \le 2^{-10}$
  and power is unchanged to within 0.001.

The constant rule is the limit of the decaying rule as
$t_{1/2} \to \infty$, applied at every positive half-life.

Power depends on the correlation profile only through the on/off
correlation difference $\mathcal G = 1 - \bar g_{\text{off}}$ (Figure
\@ref(fig:gapfig)). The difference is 1 without carryover. Under the
decaying rule in the Hybrid design it is 0.9997 at 0.1 week, 0.991 at
0.2, 0.906 at 0.5, 0.754 at 1 and 0.551 at 2. Under the constant rule
it is 0 at every positive half-life. The noncentrality is proportional
to $r_{\Delta B}/\sqrt{1 - r_{\Delta B}^2}$, and $r_{\Delta B}$ is
proportional to the difference. For small $r_{\Delta B}$ the sample
size needed for a given power therefore scales approximately as
$1/\mathcal G^2$. At 1 week this is about 1.8 times the no-carryover
sample. At 2 weeks it is about 3.3 times.

```{r gapfig, fig.cap = 'Closed-form power against the on/off correlation difference, with the positions of the two correlation rules. Hybrid design, $N = 70$, $c_{bm} = 0.25$, E9.', out.width = '75%', fig.align = 'center'}
knitr::include_graphics('../../../docs/figures/37-fig2-power-vs-gap-cov.png')
```

Replacing only the correlation lines of the starting code with the
decaying rule (Appendix B.1) and running the pipeline unchanged gave
the results in Table \@ref(tab:patch). The two versions coincide
without carryover, as they must. At 0.1 and 0.2 week the
decaying version keeps the full interaction, within Monte Carlo error
of the no-carryover value of 0.668. At 1 week it shows a gradual
decline. No matrix was repaired in either version, because
$c_{bm} = 0.25$ is below the feasibility bound.

```{r patch}
gp <- read.csv(file.path('..', '..', 'data', 'quick-sim',
                         'hendrickson-problems', 'graded-patch',
                         'graded-patch-reps500.csv'))
stopifnot(all(gp$reps == 500), all(gp$repairs == 0))
gp_pub <- gp[gp$version == 'published', ][order(gp$t_half[gp$version == 'published']), ]
gp_gr <- gp[gp$version == 'graded', ][order(gp$t_half[gp$version == 'graded']), ]
stopifnot(identical(gp_pub$t_half, gp_gr$t_half))
tab <- data.frame(th = as.character(gp_pub$t_half),
  pm = gp_pub$mean_beta, gm = gp_gr$mean_beta,
  pp = gp_pub$power, gp = gp_gr$power)
knitr::kable(tab, booktabs = TRUE, digits = 3,
  col.names = c('$t_{1/2}$ (weeks)', 'Mean estimate, constant', 'Mean estimate, decaying',
                'Power, constant', 'Power, decaying'), escape = FALSE,
  caption = paste0('The starting code at commit 58b32a9, as published (constant) and with the decaying correlation (decaying): Hybrid design, $N = 70$, $c_{bm} = 0.25$, 500 replicates per cell, same seeds. Monte Carlo SE of power at most 0.022. ', sprintf('A rerun of the original version at 0.1 week with 4,000 new replicates gave power %.3f (Stage 2 text).', m6_p)))
```

Figure \@ref(fig:fig4bmc) repeats the layout of Figure 4B of the earlier study on
the starting code, for all four designs, both sample sizes and the
five censoring patterns, as published and with the decaying
correlation. It uses $c_{bm} = 0.25$ instead of the earlier 0.6. The
value 0.6 lies above the feasibility bound of the Hybrid design and of
most cells of the other designs, so it would confound the comparison
with the repair. At 0.25 neither version
repaired a matrix, so the correlation rule is the only difference.
With 250 replicates per cell the Monte Carlo SE reaches 0.032, so a
difference of 0.05 between adjacent cells is within Monte Carlo error.
Only the pattern across cells should be read. Results at $N = 70$
without censoring:

- **Hybrid design.** Power under the constant rule falls from 0.66 to
  0.08 at both positive half-lives. Power under the decaying rule
  stays at 0.62 and 0.68.
- **Open label plus blinded discontinuation.** Power under the
  constant rule falls from 0.57 to 0.12 and 0.13. Power under the
  decaying rule stays at 0.57 and 0.60.
- **Crossover.** Power under the constant rule falls only to 0.34 and
  0.33. The placebo-first path's off-drug visits precede any exposure
  and so keep zero correlation under both rules. Power under the
  decaying rule stays at 0.71 and 0.78.
- **Open label.** There are no off-drug visits. The two rules coincide
  and power is low throughout.

The same pattern holds at $N = 35$ and under every censoring pattern.

```{r fig4bmc, fig.cap = 'Power to detect the biomarker-by-treatment interaction, in the layout of Figure 4B of the earlier study, from the starting code at commit 58b32a9 as published (upper two panel rows) and with the decaying correlation (lower two panel rows). Rows within panels: censoring patterns; columns: carryover half-life; panels: trial design (N-of-1 is the Hybrid design) and total sample size. $c_{bm} = 0.25$, 250 replicates per cell (Monte Carlo SE at most 0.032), the same seeds for both versions. No matrix was repaired in either version.', out.width = '100%', fig.align = 'center'}
knitr::include_graphics('../../figures/quick-sim/hendrickson-problems/fig4b-graded-cbm0.25.png')
```

```{r fig4bg10data}
## G10 and G9 under the starting parameters: driver 19 with
## --params published (referee report 2026-11-01, M1). The stored
## g10-planning/ and g9-planning/ runs used other response SDs and are
## not read. Until the published-set output is in place, every number
## that depends on it prints as [pending].
pub_dir <- file.path('..', '..', 'data', 'quick-sim',
                     'carryover-closed-form', 'published-planning')
pub_ok <- function(f, dir = pub_dir) {
  p <- file.path(dir, f)
  m <- file.path(dir, 'PARAM_SET')
  if (file.exists(p) && file.exists(m) &&
      identical(readLines(m, n = 1L), 'published')) p else NA_character_
}
PENDING <- '\\textbf{[pending]}'
pend <- function(have, expr) if (have) expr else PENDING
## Two rates differ when they are more than two combined Monte Carlo
## SEs apart.
rate_cmp <- function(p1, n1, p0, n0) {
  se <- sqrt(p1 * (1 - p1) / n1 + p0 * (1 - p0) / n0)
  if (abs(p1 - p0) <= 2 * se) 0L else as.integer(sign(p1 - p0))
}

f4_file <- pub_ok('fig4b-g10-cbm0.25.csv')
have_f4 <- !is.na(f4_file)
if (have_f4) g9f <- read.csv(f4_file)
f4_row <- function(d, N, th, cens = 'No censoring')
  g9f[g9f$design == d & g9f$N == N & g9f$t_half == th &
      g9f$censoring == cens, ]
g9f_pick <- function(d, N, th, cens = 'No censoring') pend(have_f4, {
  r <- f4_row(d, N, th, cens)
  stopifnot(nrow(r) == 1)
  sprintf('%.2f', r$power)
})
g9f_mcse_max <- pend(have_f4, sprintf('%.3f',
  max(sqrt(g9f$power * (1 - g9f$power) / g9f$n_conv), na.rm = TRUE)))
## Power at 0.1 and 0.2 week against the no-carryover value, N = 70,
## no censoring.
f4_cmp <- function(d) pend(have_f4, {
  r0 <- f4_row(d, 70, 0)
  s <- vapply(c(0.1, 0.2), function(th) {
    r1 <- f4_row(d, 70, th)
    k <- rate_cmp(r1$power, r1$n_conv, r0$power, r0$n_conv)
    if (k == 0L) 'within Monte Carlo error of its no-carryover value' else
      sprintf('%s (%.2f)', if (k < 0L) 'lower' else 'higher', r1$power)
  }, '')
  if (s[1] == s[2]) paste(s[1], 'at both half-lives') else
    sprintf('%s at 0.1 week and %s at 0.2 week', s[1], s[2])
})
## The censoring pattern with the lowest power, Hybrid, N = 70, 0.2 week.
f4_low <- if (have_f4) {
  r <- g9f[g9f$design == 'N-of-1' & g9f$N == 70 & g9f$t_half == 0.2 &
           g9f$censoring != 'No censoring', ]
  r[which.min(r$power), ]
} else NULL
f4_low_name <- pend(have_f4, sprintf("the '%s' pattern", f4_low$censoring))
f4_low_pow <- pend(have_f4, sprintf('%.2f', f4_low$power))
## G10 against the starting code with the decaying correlation (lower
## panels of the preceding figure) and against closed-form E9 under the
## recommended DGP, N = 70, no censoring, no carryover. Without carryover
## the two carryover rules on the mean coincide, so the figures differ
## there only in the correlation structure and the analysis.
orig_f4 <- read.csv(file.path('..', '..', 'data', 'quick-sim',
                              'hendrickson-problems', 'fig4b-graded',
                              'fig4b-graded-cbm0.25-reps250.csv'))
e9_70 <- read.csv(file.path('..', '..', 'data', 'quick-sim',
                            'carryover-closed-form', 'rho-stage',
                            'planning-n80.csv'))
f4_des <- c(`N-of-1` = 'Hybrid', `OL+BDC` = 'OL+BDC', CO = 'CO')
f4_orig <- function(d) {
  o <- orig_f4[orig_f4$version == 'graded' & orig_f4$design == d &
               orig_f4$N == 70 & orig_f4$t_half == 0 &
               orig_f4$censoring == 'No censoring', ]
  stopifnot(nrow(o) == 1)
  o
}
f4_e9 <- function(d) {
  v <- e9_70$power_N70[e9_70$design == f4_des[[d]] &
                       e9_70$c_bm == 0.25 & e9_70$t_half == 0]
  stopifnot(length(v) == 1)
  v
}
f4_trio <- function(f) pend(have_f4, sprintf('%.2f, %.2f and %.2f',
  f('N-of-1'), f('OL+BDC'), f('CO')))
f4_g10_0 <- f4_trio(function(d) f4_row(d, 70, 0)$power)
f4_orig_0 <- f4_trio(function(d) f4_orig(d)$power)
f4_e9_0 <- f4_trio(f4_e9)
## G10 below the starting code in every design, and E9 no higher than
## G10 plus two Monte Carlo SEs: the conditions the text states.
f4_all_lower <- have_f4 && all(vapply(names(f4_des), function(d) {
  g <- f4_row(d, 70, 0)
  o <- f4_orig(d)
  rate_cmp(g$power, g$n_conv, o$power, o$n) < 0
}, TRUE))
f4_e9_low <- have_f4 && all(vapply(names(f4_des), function(d) {
  g <- f4_row(d, 70, 0)
  f4_e9(d) <= g$power + 2 * sqrt(g$power * (1 - g$power) / g$n_conv)
}, TRUE))
stopifnot(!have_f4 || (f4_all_lower && f4_e9_low))
## The OL+BDC comparison at 0.2 week in the 1,000-replicate planning
## run of the same DGP and analysis.
pl_file <- pub_ok('planning-g10.csv')
f4_pl <- if (!is.na(pl_file)) {
  pl <- read.csv(pl_file)
  sapply(c(0, 0.2), function(th) {
    r <- pl[pl$design == 'OL+BDC' & pl$c_bm == 0.25 & pl$t_half == th &
            pl$N_label == '70', ]
    stopifnot(nrow(r) == 1)
    c(power = r$power, n = r$n_reps)
  })
} else NULL
f4_pl_txt <- pend(!is.null(f4_pl), {
  k <- rate_cmp(f4_pl['power', 2], f4_pl['n', 2], f4_pl['power', 1],
                f4_pl['n', 1])
  sprintf(paste('In the planning run of the same DGP and analysis, with',
                '%s replicates per cell (Table \\@ref(tab:planningg10)),',
                'OL+BDC power is %.3f without carryover and %.3f at 0.2',
                'week, %s.'),
          format(f4_pl['n', 1], big.mark = ','), f4_pl['power', 1],
          f4_pl['power', 2],
          if (k == 0) 'within Monte Carlo error of each other' else
            'a difference of more than two Monte Carlo SEs')
})
```

Figure \@ref(fig:fig4bg10) repeats the grid of Figure \@ref(fig:fig4bmc)
under the recommended DGP of Stage 7 with the analysis G10 that the
companion paper recommends [@pmsimstats-paper02]. G10 is a
random-intercept model with CAR(1) residual correlation and an
exposure-decayed drug indicator whose half-life is chosen by AIC on
the model without the interaction, with CR2 cluster-robust standard
errors (planning section). Both figures use the starting response and
baseline parameters (Methods). The data-generating process differs
from that of Figure \@ref(fig:fig4bmc) in its correlation structure
(separable AR(1) at $\rho = 0.7$ instead of compound symmetry) and in
its carryover rule on the mean, and the analysis differs, so the two
figures are not matched cell by cell. Each cell has 250 replicates and
a Monte Carlo SE of at most `r g9f_mcse_max`. The open-label design is not
estimable under G10: every visit is on drug, so the exposure-decayed
indicator is constant at 1 and the interaction term is collinear with
the biomarker. The binary-indicator analysis replaces the interaction with a
biomarker-by-time term in that case. G10 has no such substitute, and
the cells are marked as not estimable rather than simulated. The
censoring patterns in this figure use the corrected dropout rule.
The starting `censordata()` raised dropout with improvement, the
reverse of the intended mechanism, through a sign error in its biased
term (Appendix B.5). Under the corrected rule, dropout rises with
worsening. Figure \@ref(fig:fig4bmc) keeps the published rule, because
it reproduces the starting code. Results at $N = 70$ without
censoring:

- **Hybrid design.** Power is `r g9f_pick('N-of-1', 70, 0)`,
  `r g9f_pick('N-of-1', 70, 0.1)` and `r g9f_pick('N-of-1', 70, 0.2)`
  at half-lives of 0, 0.1 and 0.2 week.
- **Open label plus blinded discontinuation.** Power is
  `r g9f_pick('OL+BDC', 70, 0)`, `r g9f_pick('OL+BDC', 70, 0.1)` and
  `r g9f_pick('OL+BDC', 70, 0.2)`.
- **Crossover.** Power is `r g9f_pick('CO', 70, 0)`,
  `r g9f_pick('CO', 70, 0.1)` and `r g9f_pick('CO', 70, 0.2)`.

We compare G10 power at the pharmacological half-lives with its
no-carryover value. Two rates differ when they are more than two
combined Monte Carlo SEs apart. In the Hybrid design, power is
`r f4_cmp('N-of-1')`. In the OL+BDC design it is `r f4_cmp('OL+BDC')`.
In the crossover design it is `r f4_cmp('CO')`. Each comparison rests
on one cell of 250 replicates. `r f4_pl_txt` Of the censoring
patterns, `r f4_low_name` gives the lowest power in the Hybrid design
at 0.2 week, `r f4_low_pow`.

G10 power is lower than in the starting code with the decaying
correlation (Figure \@ref(fig:fig4bmc), lower two panel rows) in every
design. Without carryover it is `r f4_g10_0` in the Hybrid, OL+BDC and
crossover designs, against `r f4_orig_0` in the starting code. The
analysis does not account for the difference. Under the recommended DGP
the closed-form power of the paired-difference statistic E9 at the
same $N$ and $c_{bm}$ is `r f4_e9_0`, computed as for Table
\@ref(tab:planning), no higher than G10. Without carryover the two carryover rules on the mean
coincide, so the difference comes from the correlation structure. The
starting code uses compound symmetry at $\rho_{cs} = 0.8$, and the
recommended DGP uses the separable AR(1) form at $\rho = 0.7$. Table
\@ref(tab:rhostage) shows the effect of that change on closed-form E9
power in the Hybrid design. The drop is largest in the crossover
design. We have not established why.

```{r fig4bg10, eval = have_f4, fig.cap = paste0('Power of the analysis G10 to detect the biomarker-by-treatment interaction under the recommended DGP (separable AR(1), $\\rho = 0.7$, $c_1 = 0.2$, decaying correlation, carryover decaying from the last on-drug mean, original response parameters), in the layout of Figure 4B of the original study. Rows within panels: censoring patterns; columns: carryover half-life; panels: trial design (N-of-1 is the Hybrid design) and total sample size. $c_{bm} = 0.25$, 250 replicates per cell (Monte Carlo SE at most ', g9f_mcse_max, '). Censoring patterns use the corrected dropout rule, under which dropout rises with worsening; the original-code figure uses the published rule of commit 58b32a9. Gray cells (n/e): the open-label design, in which every visit is on drug and the interaction is not estimable under G10.'), out.width = '100%', fig.align = 'center', fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5.2}
library(ggplot2)
fd <- g9f
fd$design <- factor(fd$design, levels = c('OL', 'OL+BDC', 'CO', 'N-of-1'))
fd$censoring <- factor(fd$censoring,
  levels = c('high dropout', 'more of biased', 'more of flat', 'balanced',
             'No censoring'))
fd$N <- factor(paste0('N = ', fd$N), levels = c('N = 35', 'N = 70'))
fd$label <- ifelse(is.na(fd$power), 'n/e', sprintf('%.2f', fd$power))
ggplot(fd, aes(factor(t_half), censoring, fill = power)) +
  geom_tile(color = 'white') +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), size = 2.8) +
  facet_grid(N ~ design) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = 'RdYlBu', limits = c(0, 1),
                       name = 'Power', na.value = 'grey85') +
  labs(x = 'Carryover half-life (weeks)', y = 'Censoring parameters') +
  theme_grey(base_size = 10)
```

```{r fig4bg10pending, eval = !have_f4, results = 'asis'}
cat('\\begin{center}\\textbf{[Figure pending: the published-set run of',
    '19-g9-planning-and-fig4b.R, block F]}\\end{center}\n')
```

Figure \@ref(fig:fig4b) extends the comparison over interaction
strengths and longer half-lives. It shows closed-form power in the
Hybrid design for each correlation rule.

- **The constant rule.** Every column after $t_{1/2} = 0$ falls to the
  test size or just above it, at every strength. For example, at
  $c_{bm} = 0.2$ power under E9b falls from 0.46 to 0.07.
- **The decaying rule.** Power declines smoothly: 0.46, 0.46, 0.46,
  0.41, 0.32 and 0.23 at the same strength over half-lives of 0 to 2
  weeks.
- **Feasibility.** Gray cells mark effect sizes at or above the
  compound-symmetry feasibility bound, where no joint distribution
  exists. Under the decaying rule, $c_{bm} = 0.3$ becomes feasible
  only from $t_{1/2} = 1$ week. A correlation that decays instead of
  switching places a smaller demand on the structure (Appendix A.5).

```{r fig4b, fig.cap = 'Closed-form power of the paired-difference statistic by interaction strength ($c_{bm}$) and carryover half-life, in the layout of Figure 4B of the earlier study: the constant rule and the decaying correlation. Upper row: E9b, which counts baseline as an off-drug visit as the binary-indicator analysis does; lower row: E9. Gray cells: $c_{bm}$ at or above the compound-symmetry feasibility bound, where the correlation matrix is not positive definite. Hybrid design, $N = 70$, compound symmetry.', out.width = '100%', fig.align = 'center'}
knitr::include_graphics('../../../docs/figures/37-fig3-power-heatmap-cov.png')
```

The recommended DGP uses the decaying correlation. The choice rests on
identifiability under carryover and on fidelity to the pharmacology.
Two limitations of the choice are stated here. First, at the
pharmacological half-lives of 0.1 to 0.2 week the on/off correlation
difference is within 0.01 of 1. The decaying rule therefore returns the
no-carryover result. The recommended DGP at its default half-life is not
a test bed for carryover. The smooth decline is a statement about
half-lives of 0.5 week and above, which we label behavioral. Second,
the decaying correlation is asymmetric. Off drug the moderation fades
with the drug effect. On drug it is the full $c_{bm}\sigma_{BR}b_i$ at
every visit, including the first weeks of titration when the Gompertz
mean is a small fraction of its maximum. A correlation proportional to
the current drug-response mean at every visit, or a correlation
half-life separate from the mean's, would remove the asymmetry.
Neither was tried. The sensitivity model of the Discussion is the form
that addresses it. The mixed-model power of the recommended DGP at
half-lives of 0.5 to 2 weeks, with the half-life fixed in the analysis
or chosen from the data, is the subject of a companion paper
[@pmsimstats-paper02].

## Stage 3. Carryover on the mean

The compounding carryover rule decays the previous visit's mean by the
total time since discontinuation. At the second and later off-drug
visits that mean has already been decayed, so the decay compounds.
Consider two off-drug visits at weeks 11 and 12 following
discontinuation at week 10. The starting code decays the week-10 value
by $2^{-1/t_{1/2}}$ and then by $2^{-2/t_{1/2}}$, a total exponent of
3 weeks for 2 weeks elapsed. We treat the two forms as two
specifications.

The recommended DGP decays the mean from the last on-drug value,
$\mu_{BR,\text{last}}\,2^{-t_{sd}/t_{1/2}}$. The mean at any off-drug
visit then depends only on the elapsed time (Appendix B.3).

The choice changes no slope, variance or feasibility bound. It changes
only the path means. It therefore changes the closed-form power of
study 1 by at most 0.002 in the Hybrid design. In the starting
pipeline it changes power by at most 0.006. Figure \@ref(fig:trajfig)
shows the drug-response mean by visit for the four Hybrid paths under
both forms. Two features are visible. At $t_{1/2} = 1$ week the
constant rule lies below the decaying rule at the second off-drug
visit, as expected. At 0.2 week both are indistinguishable from zero
one week after discontinuation. At re-exposure (week 16 in paths 1 and
3) time on drug restarts at zero. The mean then rises along a fresh
Gompertz curve to 4.3 points at the week-16 visit, four weeks into the
restarted curve. The residual from the earlier exposure has decayed to
0.16 points by then even at a 1-week half-life. No downward step
therefore appears on the Hybrid schedule. A step would appear only if
a visit fell within about a week of re-exposure at a half-life of a
week or more.

```{r trajfig, fig.cap = 'Drug-response mean by visit in the Hybrid design, by path, under the anchored carryover rule (decay from the last on-drug mean, the recommended DGP) and the compounding carryover rule (compounded decay), at carryover half-lives of 0.2 and 1 week. Filled points: on-drug visits; open points: off-drug visits. D: drug; P: placebo.', out.width = '100%', fig.align = 'center'}
knitr::include_graphics('../../../docs/figures/01-fig-hybrid-br-mean-reexposure.png')
```

The recommended DGP decays carryover from the last on-drug mean. It keeps
the starting DGP's restart of time on drug at re-exposure, which for
prazosin matches re-titration after an interruption. For drugs without
titration the response should instead rebuild from its residual level.
That is an option, not the default. The choice rests on fidelity to
the pharmacology, as a judgment. The numerical consequence is at most
0.006 in power either way.

## Stage 4. Serial correlation

The starting DGP uses compound symmetry. Visits one week apart and
sixteen weeks apart have the same correlation of 0.8. The one PTSD
symptom series available to us, the total CAPS score in CSP 563
(planning section), has a correlation that decays slowly with lag.
Matching its 4- and 20-week correlations within this DGP's structure
would need $\rho$ of about 0.87 to 0.91 per week (Additional file 1). That
series is a total score, so it constrains the component-level $\rho$
without determining it. Both compound symmetry
and AR(1) are used in N-of-1 simulation [@chen2014]. Serial
correlation has been discussed as a design consideration for
personalized studies [@schork2022]. Two elements are open: the form of
the within-component correlation, and its value.

```{r rhobounddata}
## 24-rho-sweep.R: separable AR(1), bound by design and half-life, and
## the E9 sample size for 80 percent power by rho.
rb_dir <- file.path('..', '..', 'data', 'quick-sim', 'carryover-closed-form',
                    'rho-stage', 'rho-sweep')
rb <- read.csv(file.path(rb_dir, 'ceilings-sep.csv'))
rb_n <- read.csv(file.path(rb_dir, 'planning-n80-by-rho.csv'))
rb_min <- function(r, th) min(rb$ceiling[rb$rho == r & rb$t_half == th])
rb_bind <- function(r, th) {
  k <- rb$rho == r & rb$t_half == th
  rb$design[k][which.min(rb$ceiling[k])]
}
rb_f <- function(v) sprintf('%.3f', v)
rb_rho <- sort(unique(rb$rho))
## The Stage 4 text states these.
stopifnot(rb_rho[which.max(sapply(rb_rho, rb_min, 0))] == 0.7,
          all(sapply(rb_rho[rb_rho > 0.7], rb_bind, 0) == 'Hybrid'),
          all(diff(sapply(rb_rho[rb_rho >= 0.7], rb_min, 0)) < 0))
```

The recommended DGP uses AR(1) in calendar weeks,
$\rho^{\lvert w_t - w_s\rvert}$, with one $\rho$ for all three
components. The value of $\rho$ is a parameter. We take $\rho = 0.7$
as a convention only, not an estimate. Under the adopted separable
form an effect size of 0.3 is already feasible at
$\rho = 0.8$ (bound 0.440), so feasibility at 0.3 does not determine
the value. Of the four values in Table \@ref(tab:rhostage), 0.7 has
the largest separable feasibility bound (0.474). That keeps the
planning effect sizes feasible but says nothing about whether 0.7 is
right, and the value lies below the range the CSP 563 series suggests. Above 0.7, a larger $\rho$ lowers the feasibility bound and
raises E9 power (Table \@ref(tab:rhostage), 0.7 against 0.8). If that
continues into the range CSP 563 suggests, the planning results at
$\rho = 0.7$ overstate the largest feasible effect and the sample size
needed. Table \@ref(tab:rhobound) extends the separable form to
$\rho$ from 0.4 to 0.95. The bound is largest at $\rho = 0.7$. It
falls slowly below that value, to `r rb_f(rb_min(0.4, 0))` at 0.4, and
steeply above it, to `r rb_f(rb_min(0.9, 0))` at 0.9 and
`r rb_f(rb_min(0.95, 0))` at 0.95, where the Hybrid design is the
binding one. Above 0.7 the E9 sample size in the Hybrid design falls
as well.
The planning section repeats its calculations at $\rho = 0.5$ and 0.9.

Table \@ref(tab:rhostage) shows what $\rho$ does under compound
symmetry and under the structure adopted in Stage 5, for
$\rho \in \{0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8\}$. Under compound symmetry alone,
lowering $\rho_{cs}$ from 0.8 to 0.7 raises the feasibility bound from
0.256 to 0.346. An effect size of 0.3 then becomes feasible
by the change of $\rho$ alone, with no change of structure. The same
change lowers closed-form power at $c_{bm} = 0.25$ from 0.721 to
0.628. A lower serial correlation leaves more within-person noise in
the on-minus-off contrast. The two criteria pull in opposite
directions. The feasible range widens as $\rho$ falls, and the power
at a matched $c_{bm}$ falls.

```{r rhostage}
rs_dir <- file.path('..', '..', 'data', 'quick-sim', 'carryover-closed-form',
                    'rho-stage')
rs_ceil <- read.csv(file.path(rs_dir, 'ceilings-by-rho-min.csv'))
rs_pow <- read.csv(file.path(rs_dir, 'power-by-rho.csv'))
rs_rho <- c(0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8)
rs_get <- function(d, con, th, col, v = NULL) {
  sapply(rs_rho, function(r) {
    k <- d$rho == r & d$construct == con & d$t_half == th
    if (!is.null(v)) k <- k & d$variant == v
    stopifnot(sum(k) == 1)
    d[[col]][k]
  })
}
tab <- data.frame(
  rho = as.character(rs_rho),
  cs_ceil = rs_get(rs_ceil, 'CS', 0, 'min_ceiling'),
  cs_pow = rs_get(rs_pow, 'CS', 0, 'power', 'E9'),
  sep_ceil = rs_get(rs_ceil, 'sep', 0, 'min_ceiling'),
  sep_pow = rs_get(rs_pow, 'sep', 0, 'power', 'E9'))
rs_drop <- c(tab$cs_pow - rs_get(rs_pow, 'CS', 0.2, 'power', 'E9'),
             tab$sep_pow - rs_get(rs_pow, 'sep', 0.2, 'power', 'E9'))
knitr::kable(tab, booktabs = TRUE, digits = 3,
  col.names = c('$\\rho_{cs}$ or $\\rho$', 'Ceiling', 'Power at $c_{bm} = 0.25$',
                'Ceiling', 'Power at $c_{bm} = 0.25$'), escape = FALSE,
  caption = paste0('Serial correlation: the feasibility bound on $c_{bm}$ (Ceiling; decaying correlation, no carryover, minimum over the Hybrid, crossover and OL+BDC designs) and closed-form E9 power (Hybrid, $N = 70$, no carryover) by $\\rho$, under compound symmetry and under the separable AR(1) form of Stage 5. Under compound symmetry the Hybrid and crossover designs tie for the minimum. Under the separable form the minimum is attained in the Hybrid design at $\\rho = 0.8$ and in the OL+BDC design at $\\rho \\le 0.7$, and the crossover design is never binding. ',
                   sprintf('At $t_{1/2} = 0.2$ week every power value is lower by %.3f to %.3f.',
                           min(rs_drop), max(rs_drop)))) |>
  kableExtra::add_header_above(c(' ' = 1, 'Compound symmetry' = 2, 'Separable AR(1)' = 2))
```

```{r rhobound}
rb_hyb <- function(r, cb) {
  k <- rb_n$rho == r & rb_n$design == 'Hybrid' & rb_n$c_bm == cb &
    rb_n$t_half == 0.2
  stopifnot(sum(k) == 1)
  if (!rb_n$feasible[k]) 'not feasible' else
    if (is.na(rb_n$N80[k])) '> 2000' else as.character(rb_n$N80[k])
}
tab <- data.frame(
  rho = sprintf('%.2f', rb_rho),
  b0 = sapply(rb_rho, rb_min, 0), b02 = sapply(rb_rho, rb_min, 0.2),
  b1 = sapply(rb_rho, rb_min, 1),
  bind = ifelse(sapply(rb_rho, rb_bind, 0) == 'CO', 'Crossover',
                sapply(rb_rho, rb_bind, 0)),
  n25 = sapply(rb_rho, rb_hyb, 0.25), n35 = sapply(rb_rho, rb_hyb, 0.35))
knitr::kable(tab, booktabs = TRUE, digits = 3, escape = FALSE,
  align = 'rrrrlrr', linesep = '',
  col.names = c('$\\rho$', '$t_{1/2} = 0$', '0.2 week', '1 week',
                'Binding design', '$c_{bm} = 0.25$', '$c_{bm} = 0.35$'),
  caption = 'Serial correlation under the separable AR(1) form of the recommended DGP ($c_1 = 0.2$, decaying correlation, carryover decaying from the last on-drug mean): the feasibility bound on $c_{bm}$, minimum over the Hybrid, crossover and OL+BDC designs, by carryover half-life, the design that attains the minimum without carryover, and the closed-form total $N$ for 80 percent power of E9 in the Hybrid design at the 0.2-week half-life. Not feasible: $c_{bm}$ lies above the Hybrid bound.') |>
  kableExtra::add_header_above(c(' ' = 1, 'Feasibility bound' = 4,
                                 'Hybrid N, E9' = 2))
```

The recommended DGP uses AR(1) in weeks at $\rho = 0.7$. The choice rests
on existence, traded against power. The calibration status is open.
The AR(1) form is adopted for the reason given in Stage 5 (it is what
the analysis model assumes), not because compound symmetry has been
shown wrong for these data. Any study using the DGP should report
$\rho$. Where the conclusion could depend on it, the analysis should be
repeated at other values, as the planning section does at 0.5 and 0.9.

## Stage 5. Cross-component structure

The starting DGP has a same-visit cross-component correlation
$c_1 = 0.2$ and an other-visit correlation $c_\times = 0.1$ at every
lag. With AR(1) within components, the direct translation keeps $c_1$
at lag zero and lets the other-visit correlation decay,
$c_\times\rho^{\lvert w_t - w_s\rvert}$. This two-constant form is what
the package's `buildSigma()` builds when its two constants differ
(Appendix B.5). It is not the only choice, and it has a validity
condition.

The recommended DGP uses the separable form,
$c_1\rho^{\lvert w_t - w_s\rvert}$ at every lag including zero. The
response block is then a Kronecker product $M = K \otimes A$ of a
$3 \times 3$ component correlation $K$ (1 on the diagonal, $c_1$ off
it) and one AR(1) kernel $A_{ts} = \rho^{\lvert w_t - w_s\rvert}$. In
words, every component has the same first-order autoregressive
correlation, and the between-component correlation is constant at
every lag. It is the two-constant form with $c_\times = c_1$. The
same-visit value of the starting DGP, $c_1 = 0.2$, is kept. Four properties follow
(Appendix A.5).

1. **Validity for every schedule.** The eigenvalues of $M$ are products
   of those of $K$ and $A$, so $M$ is positive definite for any visit
   times. The two-constant form adds a same-visit cross-component term
   that carries correlation without variance. It is positive definite
   only when the smallest eigenvalue of $A$ exceeds
   $(c_1 - c_\times)/(1 - c_\times) = 0.111$. On the paper's schedules
   the condition holds (smallest eigenvalue 0.122 in the Hybrid and
   OL+BDC designs at $\rho = 0.8$, 0.193 at 0.7; 0.28 and 0.43 in the
   crossover design). On 20 weekly visits at $\rho = 0.8$ it holds by
   less than 0.001. On daily measurement over eight weeks it fails
   (0.016 at $\rho = 0.8$, 0.026 at 0.7). The two-constant form
   therefore cannot be used for the dense schedules that wearable or
   diary outcomes produce.
2. **The starting structure is already of this kind in pieces.** It is
   the sum of a person-level and an occasion-level separable term,
   each valid. This is why its matrices fail only through the
   biomarker row, never in the response block.
3. **An exact, interpretable feasibility bound.** The bound factors
   into a component term and a schedule term,
   $$
   c_{bm}^{*} = \sqrt{1 - R^2}\;\bigl(g^\top A^{-1} g\bigr)^{-1/2},
   \qquad R^2 = \frac{2c_1^2}{1 + c_1},
   $$
   where $R^2$ is the squared multiple correlation of the drug response
   on the other two components at one visit. The schedule term is a
   sum of per-step terms of the correlation profile. A profile that
   switches abruptly between closely spaced visits has a large
   per-step term. This is why designs with many on-off switches can
   carry only small effects.
4. **It nearly matches the analysis model.** Under separability the
   summed response has covariance $(s_t^\top K s_s)\,\rho^{\lvert w_t
   - w_s\rvert}$, with $s_t$ the component SDs at visit $t$ (Appendix
   A.5). With constant SDs this is exactly AR(1), the residual
   structure `corCAR1` assumes. In the Hybrid design the
   placebo-response SD is $10\eta_t$, so it halves at blinding. The
   summed-response variance is then 368 at open-label visits and 257
   at blinded visits. The correlation between an open-label and a
   blinded visit is the AR(1) value times 0.976. The summed response is
   therefore AR(1) only within a phase. Under the two-constant form it
   is, in addition, AR(1) plus a white-noise term the analysis model
   omits. These statements follow from the algebra. Their effect on
   test calibration has not been measured separately.

Table \@ref(tab:ceilings) gives the feasibility bounds. At the
starting $\rho = 0.8$ the two-constant form raises the bound only to
0.291. A single same-visit correlation repeated across visits that
share little demands more of the biomarker row. In the open-label
design, where every visit is on drug, it lowers the bound. The
separable form raises the bound to 0.440. At $\rho = 0.7$ the two
forms are close, 0.452 against 0.474. At the recommended $\rho$ the
separable form's gain in feasible range is therefore small, and its
reasons are properties 1 and 4. The bound of 0.474 is attained in the
OL+BDC design (0.480 in the Hybrid design). A correlation of 0.45 is
feasible in every design without carryover. Effects as large as
0.6 exceed every feasibility bound in the Hybrid design.

The wider feasible range has a consequence that does not depend on
the form. At the same $c_{bm}$, AR(1) data carry less information
about the interaction than compound-symmetric data. The closed-form
power of the paired-difference statistic in the Hybrid design at
$c_{bm} = 0.25$ falls from 0.721 under the starting structure to 0.335
under the separable form at $\rho = 0.8$ and 0.290 at $\rho = 0.7$. A
larger feasible correlation does not by itself mean more power. Effect
sizes under different structures should therefore be compared on the
scale of the implied slope, not of $c_{bm}$.

```{r ceilings}
cl_ceil <- read.csv(file.path('..', '..', 'data', 'quick-sim',
                              'carryover-closed-form', 'rho-stage',
                              'ceilings-by-rho-min.csv'))
cl_get <- function(r, con) {
  x <- cl_ceil$min_ceiling[cl_ceil$rho == r & cl_ceil$construct == con &
                           cl_ceil$t_half == 0]
  stopifnot(length(x) == 1)
  x
}
tab <- data.frame(rho = c('0.8', '0.7'),
                  cs = c(cl_get(0.8, 'CS'), cl_get(0.7, 'CS')),
                  f = c(cl_get(0.8, 'two'), cl_get(0.7, 'two')),
                  c = c(cl_get(0.8, 'sep'), cl_get(0.7, 'sep')))
knitr::kable(tab, booktabs = TRUE, digits = 3,
  col.names = c('$\\rho_{cs}$ or $\\rho$', 'Compound symmetry', 'AR(1), two-constant cross-component', 'Separable AR(1)'),
  escape = FALSE,
  caption = 'Largest feasible biomarker-response correlation $c_{bm}$ under the decaying correlation, without carryover, minimum over the Hybrid, crossover and OL+BDC designs. Under compound symmetry the Hybrid and crossover designs tie for the minimum. Under the two AR(1) forms the minimum is attained in the Hybrid design at $\\rho = 0.8$ and in the OL+BDC design at $\\rho = 0.7$ (separable form: Hybrid 0.480), and the crossover design is never binding.')
```

The recommended DGP uses the separable form with $c_1 = 0.2$. The choice
rests on analyzability (property 4) and existence (properties 1 and
3). The value $c_1 = 0.2$ is the starting value and is uncalibrated.

## Stage 6. Features the recommended DGP adds

The starting DGP correlates the biomarker with the drug response only.
A biomarker that is also prognostic, through an association with the
natural history, the placebo response or baseline severity, cannot be
represented. A simulation built on the starting DGP therefore cannot
show whether an analysis stays valid under such a biomarker. A
prognostic effect of the biomarker is known to bias tests of a
biomarker-by-treatment interaction when the analysis model omits or
misrepresents it [@haller2018; @kent2020path].

The recommended DGP adds optional correlations of the biomarker with the
natural-history component (constant over visits) or the
placebo-response component, a mean shift of the natural-history
component that grows along its curve, and a correlation with baseline
severity. It adds phase-specific measurement error, a Weibull
decay form and monotone dropout as further options.

**A prognostic biomarker.** We simulated a correlation of 0.3 between
the biomarker and the natural-history component, the
placebo-response component or baseline severity, and a growing mean
shift of the natural-history component of 0.3 of its SD per SD of
biomarker, with no interaction. Analyses that keep baseline as an
outcome row use one biomarker main effect $\beta_B$ for baseline and
for the off-drug visits. When the biomarker is prognostic through a
pathway that is absent at baseline, those two associations differ.
Part of the difference is attributed to the interaction (Appendix
A.4). Every analysis that shares the biomarker effect with baseline
exceeded the nominal level in at least one such cell (Table
\@ref(tab:prognostic)).

```{r stressdata}
ss_dir <- file.path('..', '..', 'data', 'quick-sim', 'carryover-closed-form',
                    'strawman-stress')
## Main run plus the two post hoc files fitted to the same trials; S is
## refitted in each post hoc file as a pairing check and dropped there.
ss_read <- function(tag) {
  x <- lapply(c('summary-full', 'summary-full-extra', 'summary-full-extra2'),
              function(b) {
    d <- read.csv(file.path(ss_dir, paste0(b, tag, '.csv')))
    if (b != 'summary-full') d <- d[d$analysis != 'S', ]
    d[, c('label', 'cbm', 'analysis', 'reject', 'fits')]
  })
  do.call(rbind, x)
}
## Third run (the reported one): the recommended DGP with fixed allocation.
## Second run: randomized allocation. First run: compounding carryover rule.
ss3 <- ss_read('-anchored-fixed-ha0.5')
ss2 <- ss_read('-anchored')
ss1 <- ss_read('')
ss_r <- function(d, lab, an, cbm = 0) {
  v <- d$reject[d$label == lab & d$cbm == cbm & d$analysis == an]
  stopifnot(length(v) == 1)
  v
}
ss_f <- function(v) sprintf('%.3f', v)
ss_list <- function(x) {
  if (length(x) < 2) return(paste(x, collapse = ''))
  paste0(paste(x[-length(x)], collapse = ', '), ' and ', x[length(x)])
}
ss_an <- c(
  R = 'Binary-indicator analysis (random intercept, model-based)',
  S = 'Random intercept + CAR(1), CR2',
  DS = 'The same, half-life chosen by AIC',
  A = 'Unstructured covariance, Kenward-Roger',
  DA = 'The same, half-life chosen by AIC',
  F1 = 'Random intercept + CAR(1) with expectancy terms, CR2',
  G1 = 'The same, with phase-specific residual variances, CR2',
  G2 = 'The same, with phase-specific residual variances, model-based',
  F1A = 'Expectancy terms, half-life chosen by AIC, CR2',
  ES = 'Random intercept + CAR(1) with free baseline slope, CR2')
ss_short <- c(R = 'the binary-indicator analysis', S = 'the CAR(1) model with CR2',
              DS = 'the CAR(1) model with AIC-chosen half-life',
              A = 'the unstructured model',
              DA = 'the unstructured model with AIC-chosen half-life',
              F1 = 'the expectancy-term model',
              G1 = 'the expectancy-term model with phase-specific variances (CR2)',
              G2 = 'the expectancy-term model with phase-specific variances (model-based)',
              F1A = 'the expectancy-term model with AIC-chosen half-life',
              ES = 'the free-baseline model')
ss_prog <- c('prog-TV-const', 'prog-TV-grow', 'prog-PB', 'prog-BL')
ss_cell <- c(`prog-TV-const` = 'the constant natural-history pathway',
             `prog-TV-grow` = 'the growing natural-history pathway',
             `prog-PB` = 'the placebo pathway',
             `prog-BL` = 'the baseline-severity pathway',
             `curve-C07` = 'the base cell', `curve-CS` = 'compound symmetry',
             `meas-error` = 'measurement error', N35 = '$N = 35$',
             N150 = '$N = 150$', thalf0 = '$t_{1/2} = 0$',
             thalf1 = '$t_{1/2} = 1$ week',
             weibull0.5 = 'Weibull decay with shape 0.5',
             weibull2 = 'Weibull decay with shape 2',
             `dropout-MCAR` = 'dropout completely at random',
             `dropout-MAR` = 'dropout dependent on the last score')
ss_tab <- function(d) {
  sapply(ss_prog, function(l) sapply(names(ss_an), function(a) ss_r(d, l, a)))
}
ss_m3 <- ss_tab(ss3)
ss_m2 <- ss_tab(ss2)
ss_m1 <- ss_tab(ss1)
ss_bold <- function(m) {
  matrix(ifelse(m > 0.075, sprintf('\\textbf{%.3f}', m), sprintf('%.3f', m)),
         nrow(m), dimnames = dimnames(m))
}
ss_band1 <- 0.05 + c(-2, 2) * sqrt(0.05 * 0.95 / 1000)
## Cells of the reported run whose classification differs from an
## earlier run, against the bold threshold (0.075) and the single-cell
## band. The first run isolates the carryover rule, the second the
## allocation.
ss_cross <- function(m, run, thr) {
  k <- which((m > thr) != (ss_m3 > thr), arr.ind = TRUE)
  if (!nrow(k)) return('none')
  paste(sprintf('%s under %s (%s run %s, third run %s)',
                ss_short[rownames(ss_m3)[k[, 1]]],
                ss_cell[colnames(ss_m3)[k[, 2]]], run,
                ss_f(m[k]), ss_f(ss_m3[k])), collapse = '; ')
}
ss_dmax_at <- function(m) {
  d <- abs(ss_m3 - m)
  k <- which(d == max(d), arr.ind = TRUE)[1, ]
  sprintf('%s, for %s under %s', ss_f(max(d)),
          ss_short[rownames(ss_m3)[k[1]]], ss_cell[colnames(ss_m3)[k[2]]])
}
## Pooled size over the 11 non-prognostic null cells.
ss_np <- c('curve-C07', 'curve-CS', 'meas-error', 'N35', 'N150', 'thalf0',
           'thalf1', 'weibull0.5', 'weibull2', 'dropout-MCAR', 'dropout-MAR')
ss_pool <- function(d, an) {
  x <- d[d$cbm == 0 & d$label %in% ss_np & d$analysis == an, ]
  stopifnot(nrow(x) == 11)
  sum(x$reject * x$fits) / sum(x$fits)
}
ss_cmax <- function(d, an) {
  x <- d[d$cbm == 0 & d$label %in% ss_np & d$analysis == an, ]
  x[which.max(x$reject), ]
}
ss_band11 <- 2 * sqrt(0.05 * 0.95 / 11000)
## Only analyses defined in the paper (Table tab:prognostic).
ss_fixed <- c('S', 'F1', 'ES', 'G1')
ss_fixed_pool <- sapply(ss_fixed, function(a) ss_pool(ss3, a))
ss_fixed_max <- max(sapply(ss_fixed, function(a) ss_cmax(ss3, a)$reject))
ss_all <- c('R', 'S', 'C1', 'C2', 'DS', 'A', 'DA', 'F1', 'F2', 'ES', 'EA',
            'G1', 'G2', 'F1A')
ss_above <- ss_all[sapply(ss_all, function(a) ss_pool(ss3, a)) > 0.05 + ss_band11]
## The Changes-between-runs text states these for all three runs.
for (m in list(ss_m1, ss_m2, ss_m3)) {
  stopifnot(all(m[c('F1', 'G1', 'G2', 'F1A'), ] < ss_band1[2]),
            all(apply(m[c('R', 'S', 'DS', 'A', 'DA'), ], 1, max) >
                ss_band1[2]),
            max(m['ES', ]) < ss_band1[2] + 0.015)
}
stopifnot(max(ss_m1['ES', ]) < ss_band1[2],
          which.max(ss_m2['ES', ]) == 2, max(ss_m2['ES', ]) > ss_band1[2],
          which.max(ss_m3['ES', ]) == 2, max(ss_m3['ES', ]) > ss_band1[2])
```

```{r prognostic}
tab <- data.frame(Analysis = unname(ss_an), ss_bold(ss_m3), check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(tab, booktabs = TRUE, escape = FALSE, row.names = FALSE,
  linesep = '',
  col.names = c('Analysis', 'Natural history, constant', 'Natural history, growing',
                'Placebo response', 'Baseline severity'),
  caption = 'Null rejection rates under a prognostic biomarker ($c_{bm} = 0$). Each pathway has strength 0.3: a correlation of 0.3 with the natural-history component (constant), the placebo-response component or baseline severity, and for the growing natural-history pathway a mean shift of the natural-history component of 0.3 of its SD (3 points) per SD of biomarker at the end of its curve, growing along the curve. 1,000 replicates per cell (two-MCSE band 0.036 to 0.064 for a single cell). Third run of study 3: the recommended DGP, with carryover decaying from the last on-drug mean and fixed path allocation. Rates above 0.075 in bold. The first run is in Table \\ref{tab:prognosticfirst}; the changes between runs are given in the text.') |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(font_size = 9) |>
  kableExtra::column_spec(1, width = '5.5cm') |>
  kableExtra::column_spec(2:5, width = '2.1cm')
```

The expectancy-term family stayed within the single-cell two-MCSE band
in every prognostic cell. Its four analyses rejected
`r ss_f(min(ss_m3[c('F1', 'G1', 'G2', 'F1A'), ]))` to
`r ss_f(max(ss_m3[c('F1', 'G1', 'G2', 'F1A'), ]))`. This family adds
the expectancy and a biomarker-by-expectancy term to the mean model,
with or without residual variances that differ by trial phase. The
free-baseline model adds `bmc:bl0`, which gives baseline its own
biomarker slope. It rejected `r ss_f(ss_m3['ES', 'prog-TV-grow'])`
under the growing natural-history pathway, above the single-cell band,
and `r ss_f(ss_m3['ES', 'prog-PB'])` under the placebo pathway.
Appendix A.4 explains why freeing the baseline slope alone is not
sufficient when the prognostic slope grows over time or scales with
the expectancy. A prognostic association with baseline severity alone
did less harm, because baseline severity enters every visit equally.
The binary-indicator analysis rejected `r ss_f(ss_m3['R', 'prog-BL'])` there.
The scenarios in
which the pathway is absent at baseline are the ones that show the
inflation. Whether such a pathway, at a magnitude of 0.3, is realistic
for blood pressure in PTSD is not known, but a DGP that cannot
generate it cannot show the inflation.

**Changes between runs.** Study 3 was run three times (Methods). The
reported run differs from the first only in the carryover rule, and
from the second only in the allocation. Treating two runs as
independent, the difference between them in one cell has a Monte Carlo
SE of about 0.010 at a rate of 0.05. The first and third runs use the
same seeds and allocation, so their differences are paired and that
SE overstates their noise.

The carryover rule changed the prognostic table by at most
`r ss_dmax_at(ss_m1)` (Appendix C, Table \@ref(tab:prognosticfirst)).
Cells that crossed the bold threshold of 0.075:
`r ss_cross(ss_m1, 'first', 0.075)`. Cells that crossed the upper edge
of the single-cell band: `r ss_cross(ss_m1, 'first', ss_band1[2])`.

Randomized allocation changed it by at most `r ss_dmax_at(ss_m2)`.
Cells that crossed the bold threshold:
`r ss_cross(ss_m2, 'second', 0.075)`. Cells that crossed the upper edge
of the single-cell band: `r ss_cross(ss_m2, 'second', ss_band1[2])`.
In all three runs the expectancy-term family stayed within the
single-cell band in every prognostic cell, and the binary-indicator, CAR(1) and
unstructured analyses, with or without an AIC-chosen half-life, exceeded
it in at least one. Taken analysis by analysis, only the free-baseline
model changed its classification. It stayed within the band in the
first run and exceeded it under the growing pathway in the other two,
by at most
`r ss_f(max(ss_m2['ES', ], ss_m3['ES', ]) - ss_band1[2])`.

**Feasibility with a prognostic correlation.** A prognostic
correlation occupies the same biomarker row of the correlation matrix
as $c_{bm}$. The two therefore share one feasibility condition.
Writing the row as a sum of fixed patterns scaled by the correlations,
the existence condition of Stage 1 becomes a quadratic form. The
largest value of one correlation given the others is the positive
root of a quadratic (Appendix A.4). Table \@ref(tab:jointceiling)
gives the bounds for the Hybrid design under the recommended DGP. At the
stress test's half-life of 0.5 week, the prognostic correlation of 0.3
used above lies inside the feasible region at every $c_{bm}$ up to
0.45, by 0.006 at 0.45. At 0.2 week it is feasible only up to
$c_{bm} = 0.42$. A prognostic correlation of 0.6 is
infeasible with any $c_{bm}$. That is the combination the companion
study's two repaired runs had simulated (Stage 1). The correlations
with the placebo-response and the natural-history components have
identical bounds, because their patterns are the same constant on
every visit of one component. A correlation with baseline severity
has a looser bound, since baseline severity is uncorrelated with the
response components and enters only through its square. The OL+BDC
bounds are within 0.035 of the Hybrid values. The crossover bounds are
looser on $c_{bm}$ and $c_{BL}$, and slightly tighter on $c_{PB}$
alone (0.487 against 0.513). We verified the bounds by checking that the
smallest eigenvalue of the full matrix is positive at 0.999 times each
bound and negative at 1.001 times it.

```{r jointceiling}
jc <- read.csv(file.path('..', '..', 'data', 'quick-sim',
                         'carryover-closed-form', 'rho-stage',
                         'prognostic-joint-ceilings.csv'))
hyb <- jc[jc$design == 'Hybrid' & jc$t1half %in% c(0.2, 0.5), ]
rows <- data.frame(
  coupling = c('$c_{PB}$ or $c_{TV}$', '', '', '', '$c_{BL}$', '', '', '',
               '$c_{bm}$', '', ''),
  given = c('alone', '$c_{bm} = 0.25$', '$c_{bm} = 0.30$', '$c_{bm} = 0.45$',
            'alone', '$c_{bm} = 0.25$', '$c_{bm} = 0.30$', '$c_{bm} = 0.45$',
            'alone', '$c_{PB} = 0.3$', '$c_{PB} = 0.6$'),
  key_c = c(rep('c_pb', 4), rep('c_bl', 4), rep('c_bm', 3)),
  key_g = c('alone', 'c_bm = 0.25', 'c_bm = 0.3', 'c_bm = 0.45',
            'alone', 'c_bm = 0.25', 'c_bm = 0.3', 'c_bm = 0.45',
            'alone', 'c_pb = 0.3', 'c_pb = 0.6'))
pick <- function(th) {
  sapply(seq_len(nrow(rows)), function(i) {
    v <- hyb$ceiling[hyb$t1half == th & hyb$coupling == rows$key_c[i] &
                     hyb$given == rows$key_g[i]]
    if (length(v) != 1 || is.na(v)) 'none' else sprintf('%.3f', v)
  })
}
tab <- data.frame(rows$coupling, rows$given, pick(0.2), pick(0.5))
knitr::kable(tab, booktabs = TRUE, escape = FALSE, linesep = '',
  col.names = c('Correlation', 'Given', '$t_{1/2} = 0.2$ week', '$t_{1/2} = 0.5$ week'),
  caption = 'Largest feasible prognostic correlation given the biomarker-response correlation, and the reverse, under the recommended DGP (separable AR(1), $\\rho = 0.7$, $c_1 = 0.2$), Hybrid design, minimum over its four paths. Correlation: the quantity whose bound is given. $c_{PB}$, $c_{TV}$, $c_{BL}$: correlation of the biomarker with the placebo-response component, the natural-history component and baseline severity. None: no value is feasible.')
```

```{r optdata}
op_lab <- c('curve-C07', 'meas-error', 'dropout-MCAR', 'dropout-MAR',
            'weibull0.5', 'weibull2', 'thalf0', 'thalf1', 'N35', 'N150')
op_an <- c('R', 'S', 'F1')
op_get <- function(d, cbm) {
  sapply(op_an, function(a) sapply(op_lab, function(l) ss_r(d, l, a, cbm)))
}
op_n2 <- op_get(ss3, 0)
op_p2 <- op_get(ss3, 0.3)
op_n1 <- op_get(ss1, 0)
op_p1 <- op_get(ss1, 0.3)
## Change in power from the base cell, phrased by its sign.
op_chg <- function(lab) {
  v <- op_p2[lab, ] - op_p2['curve-C07', ]
  r <- sprintf('%.2f to %.2f', min(abs(v)), max(abs(v)))
  if (all(v < 0)) paste('lowered power by', r)
  else if (all(v >= 0)) paste('raised power by', r)
  else sprintf('changed power by %+.2f to %+.2f', min(v), max(v))
}
op_rng <- function(x) sprintf('%.2f to %.2f', min(x), max(x))
op_valid_max <- max(op_n2[, c('S', 'F1')])
op_valid_k <- which(op_n2[, c('S', 'F1')] == op_valid_max, arr.ind = TRUE)[1, ]
op_valid_an <- c('S', 'F1')[op_valid_k[2]]
op_valid_at <- ss_cell[rownames(op_n2)[op_valid_k[1]]]
op_R_max <- max(op_n2[, 'R'])
op_R_at <- ss_cell[rownames(op_n2)[which.max(op_n2[, 'R'])]]
```

**Size more generally.** We pooled the 11 non-prognostic null cells
(11,000 replicates). The nominal band is 0.05 plus or minus two Monte
Carlo SE, $2\sqrt{0.05 \times 0.95 / 11{,}000} = 0.004$, that is
`r ss_f(0.05 - ss_band11)` to `r ss_f(0.05 + ss_band11)`. The binary-indicator
analysis rejected `r ss_f(ss_pool(ss3, 'R'))`, and
`r ss_f(ss_r(ss3, 'N35', 'R'))` at $N = 35$. The unstructured model
with Kenward-Roger inference [@kenward1997] rejected
`r ss_f(ss_pool(ss3, 'A'))`, with `r ss_f(ss_r(ss3, 'N35', 'A'))` at
$N = 35$. Random-intercept models with continuous-time AR(1) residuals
and CR2 cluster-robust standard errors [@bell2002; @pustejovsky2018],
at the fixed analysis half-life, rejected
`r ss_f(min(ss_fixed_pool))` to `r ss_f(max(ss_fixed_pool))`. No single
cell of these models exceeded `r ss_f(ss_fixed_max)`. With the
half-life chosen by AIC, the CAR(1) model rejected
`r ss_f(ss_pool(ss3, 'DS'))` and the expectancy-term model
`r ss_f(ss_pool(ss3, 'F1A'))`. The latter's largest single cell was
`r ss_f(ss_cmax(ss3, 'F1A')$reject)`, under
`r ss_cell[ss_cmax(ss3, 'F1A')$label]`. Of the analyses in this
paragraph, `r ss_list(ss_short[intersect(c('R', 'A', 'DS', 'F1A'), ss_above)])`
lie above the pooled band. Single-cell flags should be judged against
the number of comparisons. With `r length(ss_an)` reported analyses and 15
null cells, about
`r round(length(ss_an) * 15 * 2 * pnorm(-2))` analysis-cell pairs would
fall outside a two-MCSE band by chance at nominal size. The pairs are
not independent, since all analyses share the same trials. A single
exceedance, such as the free-baseline model under the growing pathway,
is therefore weak evidence on its own.

**The options.** Table \@ref(tab:options) shows what each optional
feature did to size and power for three analyses: the binary-indicator
analysis, the random-intercept CAR(1) model with CR2, and the
expectancy-term model that the prognostic cells favor. Measurement
error (SD 3 open label, 6 blinded) `r op_chg('meas-error')`. Dropout
of 20% completely at random `r op_chg('dropout-MCAR')`. Dropout of
20% dependent on the last score `r op_chg('dropout-MAR')`. A Weibull
decay with the same half-life `r op_chg('weibull0.5')` at shape 0.5
(a steep early decay) and `r op_chg('weibull2')` at shape 2. The true
half-life itself moved power from `r op_rng(op_p2['thalf0', ])` at
zero to `r op_rng(op_p2['thalf1', ])` at one week. Halving $N$ gave
power of `r op_rng(op_p2['N35', ])`, against
`r op_rng(op_p2['curve-C07', ])` in the base cell. At $N = 150$ the
CAR(1) model reached `r sprintf('%.2f', op_p2['N150', 'S'])`. In these
null cells the CAR(1) and expectancy-term models rejected at most
`r ss_f(op_valid_max)`, against a single-cell band of
`r ss_f(ss_band1[1])` to `r ss_f(ss_band1[2])``r if (op_valid_max > ss_band1[2]) sprintf(' (the maximum, for %s under %s, lies %s above the upper edge)', ss_short[op_valid_an], op_valid_at, ss_f(op_valid_max - ss_band1[2])) else ''`.
The binary-indicator analysis rejected up to `r ss_f(op_R_max)`, under
`r op_R_at`. The features change power, which the planning section
and the companion paper address.

           'Measurement error (SD 3 and 6)',
           'Dropout 20 percent, completely at random',
           'Dropout 20 percent, dependent on last score',
           'Weibull decay, shape 0.5',
           'Weibull decay, shape 2', '$t_{1/2} = 0$', '$t_{1/2} = 1$ week',

  n_R = op_n2[, 'R'], n_S = op_n2[, 'S'], n_F = op_n2[, 'F1'],
  p_R = op_p2[, 'R'], p_S = op_p2[, 'S'], p_F = op_p2[, 'F1'])
knitr::kable(tab, booktabs = TRUE, digits = 3, escape = FALSE, row.names = FALSE,
  col.names = c('Cell', 'Binary', 'CAR(1)', 'Expect.',
                'Binary', 'CAR(1)', 'Expect.'),
  linesep = '',
  caption = 'The optional features of the recommended DGP: null rejection rate ($c_{bm} = 0$; 1,000 replicates, MCSE 0.007) and power ($c_{bm} = 0.30$; 500 replicates, MCSE at most 0.022) for the binary-indicator analysis (Binary), the random-intercept CAR(1) model with CR2 and the expectancy-term model with CR2 (Expect.). Hybrid design, third run of study 3 (the recommended DGP: carryover decaying from the last on-drug mean, fixed allocation). Each row changes one feature of the base cell.') |>
  kableExtra::add_header_above(c(' ' = 1, 'Null rejection' = 3, 'Power' = 3)) |>
